title: Scalable Top-Down Fabrication of InP Nanopillars Using Random Mask Technique
author: Soo, Narangari, et al.
materials: Sapphire wafer (101.6 mm diameter, 1.0 mm thickness)

steps.title: Clean wafer before SiO₂ deposition
steps.instruction: Blow‑dry a clean p‑type InP wafer with a nitrogen gun.

steps.title: Deposit 400 nm SiO₂ by PECVD
steps.instruction: Load the wafer onto the metallic carrier in the PECVD load‑lock, then deposit a 400 nm SiO₂ layer on both sides using 81 sccm N₂, 355 sccm N₂O and 4.8 sccm SiH₄ at 300 °C, 20 W RF power, 650 mTorr chamber pressure. Perform a dummy run beforehand and calibrate the SiO₂ growth rate with ellipsometry.

substeps.instruction: Allow the wafer to cool before removing it from the chamber; wait a few minutes and use metal tweezers to avoid burns and plastic‑tweezer softening.

steps.title: Deposit 10 nm Au by e‑beam evaporation
steps.instruction: Blow‑dry the SiO₂‑coated wafer, load it immediately into the electron‑beam evaporator, pump to 9 × 10⁻⁶ Torr, then evaporate 10 nm Au at 0.5 Å s⁻¹ while rotating the wafer holder at 50 rpm.

substeps.instruction: Monitor Au thickness continuously; any deviation alters nano‑dot density and size.
Allow the evaporation boat and system to cool before retrieving the Au‑deposited wafer.

steps.title: Rapid thermal anneal to form Au nano‑dots
steps.instruction: Blow‑dry the Au‑SiO₂ wafer, place it immediately on the RTA graphite sample holder, and anneal at 450 °C for 9 min under a flow of 500 sccm Ar/N₂. Cool the wafer before removal.

substeps.instruction: Perform a dummy anneal without a sample beforehand.
Ensure SiO₂ layers are pin‑hole free to protect the InP from decomposition above 500 °C.

steps.title: Clean RIE chamber with Ar/O₂ plasma
steps.instruction: Run a 10 min plasma cleaning at room temperature (22‑25 °C) under 100 mTorr using a 100 sccm Ar/O₂ gas mixture with 200 W RF power.

steps.title: Etch SiO₂ around Au nano‑dots
steps.instruction: Blow‑dry the annealed wafer, load it into the RIE chamber, pre‑condition the chamber with the same SiO₂ etch parameters, then pump to 30 mTorr and etch SiO₂ with CHF₃ plasma for 13 min 30 s at room temperature, 200 W RF power, 25 sccm CHF₃.

steps.title: Calibrate SiO₂ etch rate (optional)
steps.instruction: Etch a bare SiO₂ test wafer for 5 min under the same CHF₃ conditions, measure thickness before and after with ellipsometry, and compute the etch rate (nm min⁻¹) to avoid over‑ or under‑etching of real samples.

steps.title: Inspect random Au/SiO₂ mask
steps.instruction: Examine the processed wafer with a scanning electron microscope to assess the morphology and dimensions of the self‑assembled Au/SiO₂ random mask.

description: Top-down fabrication method can be used to fabricate semiconductor nanopillars (NPs) with controlled dimensions, density with predefined doping, and heterostructures; which is challenging to achieve using bottom-up growth methods. The top-down method involves etching the material around the pre-patterned mask using either chemical or plasma etching. The anisotropic nature of plasma etching helps to achieve high aspect ratio NPs in the top-down approach. However, applying top-down fabrication of NPs is hindered due to the necessity of using complex, scalable, and expensive lithography masking techniques. Here, we developed a simple and scalable methodology, which constitutes self-assembled random mask technique and inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP-RIE), for top-down fabrication of wafer-scale III-V semiconductor NPs. In this technique, a deposited thin metal film undergoes dewetting to form self-assembled random metal nano-dots when annealed at higher temperature. These randomly formed metal nano-dots are used as an etch mask for top-down fabrication of semiconductor NPs. The protocol below describes the specific steps involved in top-down fabrication of InP NPs using ICP-RIE and self-assembled random mask technique. This protocol consists of three sections (a) development of hard self-assembled Au/SiO2 random nano-mask using self-assembled random mask technique, (b) fabrication and plasma damage removal of InP NPs, and (c) fabrication and demonstration of InP NP photocathodes for photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting. Here, we used a commercial 350 μm, Vertical Gradient Freeze-grown, p-type InP wafer (zinc-doped, orientation) for fabrication of InP NPs. However, we have also used this protocol for fabrication of other III-V semiconductor NPs such as GaN, InGaN/GaN and GaAs, as well as Si.
